questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation of the tangent to the curve $\left(1+x^2\right) y=2-x$, where it crosses the $x$-axis, is
questions.solution:
The given equation of curve is $\left(1+x^2\right) y=2-x$, it meets $x$-axis at $(2,0)$ or it can be rewritten as $y=\frac{2-x}{1+x^2}$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
\frac{d y}{d x} & =\frac{\left(1+x^2\right)(-1)-(2-x)(2 x)}{\left(1+x^2\right)^2} \\
& =\frac{-1-x^2-4 x+2 x^2}{\left(1+x^2\right)^2} \\
\Rightarrow\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)_{(2,0)} & =\frac{-1-4-8+8}{25}=-\frac{1}{5}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Required equation of tangent is
$(y-0)=-\frac{1}{5}(x-2) \Rightarrow x+5 y=2$

questions.q: The function $y=a(1-\cos x)$ is maximum when $x$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, $y=a(1-\cos x)$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\frac{d y}{d x}=a \sin x$
Again differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=a \cos x$
Put $\frac{d y}{d x}=0$ for maxima or minima
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow  a \sin x=0 \Rightarrow x=\pi \\
& \therefore \left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)_{x=\pi}=a \cos \pi=-a
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Function is maximum at $x=\pi$.

questions.q: The area bounded by the curve $y=x^4-2 x^3+x^2+3$ with $x$-axis and ordinates corresponding to the minima of $y$ is
questions.solution:
The equation of given curve is
$y=x^4-2 x^3+x^2+3$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\frac{d y}{d x}=4 x^3-6 x^2+2 x$
Again, differentiating, we get
$\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=12 x^2-12 x+2$
Put, $\frac{d y}{d x}=0$ for maxima or minima.

and $\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)_{x=1}=12-12+2=2\therefore$ Function is minimum at $x=1$
Also, $\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)_{\left(x=\frac{1}{2}\right)}=-1 \lt 0\therefore$ Function is maximum at $x=\frac{1}{2}\therefore$ Required area $=\int_0^1\left(x^4-2 x^3+x^2+3\right) d x=\left[\frac{x^5}{5}-\frac{2 x^4}{4}+\frac{x^3}{3}+3 x\right]_0^1\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+3 \\ & =\frac{91}{30} \text { sq unit }\end{aligned}$

questions.q: In the set $Q^{+}$of all positive rational numbers, the operation * is defined by the formula $a * b=\frac{a b}{6}$. Then, the inverse of 9 with respect
questions.solution:
Let $e$ be the identity.
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore a * e=a \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{a b}{6}=a \\
& \Rightarrow e=6 \\
& \because a * a^{-1}=e \\
& \therefore a * a^{-1}=6 \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{a a^{-1}}{6}=6 \Rightarrow a^{-1}=\frac{6 \times 6}{a} \\
& \therefore 9^{-1}=\frac{6 \times 6}{9}=4
\end{aligned}$

From Coulomb's law
$\begin{aligned}

& =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q^2}{2}\left[-\frac{4 a x}{\left(a^2-x^2\right)^2}\right]
\end{aligned}$
When $x\lt \lt a$, then
$\begin{aligned}
& F=-\frac{2 q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 a^3} x \\
\Rightarrow & F \propto-x
\end{aligned}$
Hence, SHM along $x$-axis.

Using red light $(\lambda=6600 Å) 60$ fringes are seen.
Hence, range of field of view is
$60 \times w=60 \times \frac{D \lambda}{d}$
Using light of wavelength $\lambda^{\prime}, n$ fringes are seen, then
$\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow  60 \times \frac{D \lambda}{d} & =n \times \frac{D \lambda^{\prime}}{d} \\
60 \times \lambda & =n \times \lambda^{\prime} \\
\Rightarrow  n=60 \times \frac{\lambda}{\lambda^{\prime}} & =60 \times \frac{6600}{4400}=90
\end{aligned}$

$F=\frac{d p}{d t} \Rightarrow p=F d t$
where $p=$ momentum $=m v\therefore m v=F d t\Rightarrow v=\frac{F d t}{m}$
Given, $F=20 \mathrm{~N}, d t=2 \mathrm{~s}, m=2 \mathrm{~kg}\therefore v=\frac{20 \times 2}{2}=20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$
Work done $=\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times(20)^2=400 \mathrm{~J}$
